case_studies.title: A Controlled Experimental Evaluation of Configuration and Cache Architecture in LLM Serving Engines
case_studies.abstract: Multi-agent LLM applications repeat most of their prompt tokens across requests, and serving engines reuse the cached state of shared prefixes. vLLM and SGLang reuse it at different granularities, and benchmarks of their default deployments report large performance gaps, usually credited to the cache. Such comparisons rarely control for other configuration differences. One of them, whether a long prompt is prefilled in chunks, is set by each engine's defaults from the hardware and the release, and it confounds the comparison. We built a reproducible testbed on Kubernetes and a seeded multi-agent workload generator, and compared the two engines under vendor defaults and with chunked prefill matched. SGLang's configuration is the same in both arms, which makes it an internal control across independently provisioned deployments. Under defaults, vLLM's median time to first token is up to 64x SGLang's. Matching one setting removes 78% of the capacity gap where that gap is largest and 30 to 67% of the latency gap. Near saturation the remaining latency gap reflects queue growth. A fluid queue model driven only by a 4.4% throughput shortfall reproduces it, and shows that such a gap scales with the length of the benchmark run. What survives matching is a tail-latency advantage of 2.4 to 6.4x at equal throughput, consistent with cache-aware ordering of waiting requests. We derive six recommendations for comparing serving engines.
case_studies.summary: The study shows that LLM serving engines like vLLM and SGLang can differ wildly in performance because of configuration settings, especially how they prefill long prompts. By creating a controlled Kubernetes testbed and matching a key setting (chunked prefill), the researchers cut the biggest performance gaps and uncovered a real tail‑latency advantage for cache‑aware engines. This means that if you run LLM services, a small configuration tweak can give you up to 6× better worst‑case latency.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage LLM inference on Kubernetes, check the prefill setting in your engine: 1) Identify if you use chunked or single‑prefill for long prompts; 2) Align this setting across all engine versions you run; 3) Measure median first‑token latency and tail latency before and after the change to confirm improvement.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents concrete benchmarking results for LLM serving engines on Kubernetes, directly informing infrastructure decisions for IT engineers deploying LLM workloads. The work uses released code and a reproducible testbed, indicating practical maturity. The findings can be leveraged to optimize service costs and performance, enabling near‑term commercial deployment or internal service improvements, justifying a high monetisation score.

case_studies.title: Enabling AWS Cloud FPGA Development Using High-Level Vitis HLS
case_studies.abstract: We present a toolchain for development of ML models on AWS EC2 F2 cloud FPGA infrastructure from high-level language, implementing a complete Vitis HLS to HDK bridge to AFI workflow that has been absent from the academic literature despite eight years of AWS FPGA availability. We introduce a four-level methodology (FP32 PyTorch, bit-accurate quantized Python, HLS C-simulation, physical FPGA) to aid in localizing errors, including FPGA-specific circuit errors. Together these tools allow coding agents to effectively implement FPGA designs from user directions, testing and debugging as needed. We document the deployment workflow, timing closure strategies, and practical HLS engineering decisions that proved crucial. We validate using TinyBERT fine-tuned for address Named Entity Recognition, implementing the embedding layer and the first of four encoder layers on the FPGA hardware. Our implementation streams weights from host DRAM, yielding poor performance compared to CPU/GPU implementations; we discuss forward paths.
case_studies.summary: This research builds a full toolchain that lets developers write high‑level ML code in PyTorch, convert it to Vitis HLS C, then to an AWS EC2 F2 FPGA image, and run it on cloud FPGAs. It solves the gap of a complete workflow from code to FPGA on AWS, demonstrating a TinyBERT encoder layer running on a cloud FPGA. The result shows the pipeline works but current performance is worse than CPUs/GPU, indicating room for optimisation.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage AWS EC2 F2 FPGAs, check the new Vitis HLS to AFI workflow to shorten your development cycle: 1) develop and test your model in PyTorch, 2) quantise and export to Python, 3) use the provided bridge to generate HLS C and compile to an AFI image, then 4) deploy on EC2 F2 instances. This can reduce time-to-market for ML acceleration on AWS cloud FPGAs.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a concrete toolchain for developing ML models on AWS FPGA instances, directly impacting engineers managing AWS cloud infrastructure. The methodology and validation on a real model suggest a usable system, though performance is limited, indicating moderate maturity. The approach offers a potential quick deployment service for specialized inference workloads, but commercial viability within 90 days is limited, hence a modest monetisation score.

case_studies.title: CompressionBench: How can your coding agents compress LLMs?
case_studies.abstract: Recursive self-improvement requires AI systems to improve the models and infrastructure used by subsequent systems. LLM compression offers a concrete efficiency objective: retain a pretrained model's behavior within a smaller model storage budget. We study whether coding agents can carry out this step autonomously. We formulate compression as a terminal task in which an agent receives a source checkpoint, storage limit, inference environment, and time budget, then constructs compressed weights and executable inference code. The agent controls its algorithm and experiments; perplexity feedback guides search, and independent verification checks the final model. Across six agents and six model--size settings, 29 of 36 submissions pass verification. Selecting the lowest-perplexity agent design per task yields an average 3.4% perplexity increase over BF16 and 77.33% downstream accuracy, compared with 79.56% for BF16. Recorded experiments reveal how agents achieve these outcomes and where improvement breaks down. Agents lower PPL in 21 of 24 revisions at nearly fixed storage; complete-model feedback reverses 17 of 79 prior local rankings; and generation and inference tests expose failures that likelihood alone misses. The results identify representation design, experimental judgment, and capability validation as central to agent-driven model compression, a measurable component of efficiency-oriented self-improvement.
case_studies.summary: This research tackles the problem of fitting large language models into limited storage by using autonomous coding agents to compress them. The authors built agents that take a source checkpoint, a storage limit, and a time budget, then generate compressed weights and inference code, achieving a 3.4 % higher perplexity than BF16 while keeping downstream accuracy at 77.3 %. The result shows that automated agent‑driven compression can reliably reduce model size without severe accuracy loss.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure, here is what to do: 1) assess your LLM deployments against storage and cost limits; 2) use or deploy a coding agent to compress models to your budget; 3) validate the compressed model with perplexity and downstream tests before rolling out to production.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper demonstrates an automated approach to compress LLMs via coding agents, which could reduce storage and inference costs for IT teams. While the system is experimentally validated, it remains in the research phase and lacks a production-ready pipeline, hence moderate maturity. The technique has clear commercial value for cloud or SaaS providers looking to offer lightweight models, giving a moderate monetisation potential. Overall, it has a meaningful but not immediate impact on everyday IT engineering.

case_studies.title: SpecCompact: Accelerating LLM Agent Context Compaction with Slot-Parallel Semantic Speculative Verification
case_studies.abstract: LLM agents use context compaction to manage growing interaction histories, but summarizing long histories with large models can introduce substantial delays. Compaction therefore requires balancing information retention against latency. We observe that structured summary slots can retain information when generated independently. Based on this observation, we present SpecCompact, a framework that accelerates compaction through slot-parallel semantic speculation. SpecCompact fine-tunes a small drafter and generates slots in parallel. The target model verifies each proposed line and repairs rejected content, while subsequent drafting uses the updated slot prefix. System optimizations further reduce repeated context processing and model calls. Across AppWorld and $τ^3$ benchmarks with two target models, SpecCompact achieves $2.04$--$5.63\times$ compaction speedups over Hermes-style summarization. Separate downstream evaluations reveal model- and task-dependent performance trade-offs. A user study within Hermes further shows an $8.68\times$ median compaction speedup.
case_studies.summary: SpecCompact speeds up how large language model agents condense long interaction histories by drafting summary slots in parallel and having the main model verify them. It cuts compaction time up to 5.6× compared to traditional summarisation, keeping the same level of information. This could reduce the latency of LLM‑driven services that rely on quick context summarisation.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage LLM‑based services, implement SpecCompact by (1) training a small draft model to produce slot summaries in parallel, (2) letting your main model validate and correct each slot, and (3) integrating the verified slots back into the conversation history. Monitor the trade‑off between speed and accuracy for your specific tasks.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper proposes a novel method to accelerate context compaction for LLM agents, which can reduce latency and compute costs—relevant to IT infrastructure teams. It presents a working framework with reported speedups, indicating some level of maturity, but lacks evidence of production deployment. The technique could be packaged as a service or integrated into existing AI pipelines, offering modest short‑term monetisation potential.

case_studies.title: MCP-Eco: A Linked Dataset of MCP Servers, Consumers, and Development Activity
case_studies.abstract: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) enables LLM agents to access external tools and data. Studying its software ecosystem requires connecting server interfaces, the projects that configure these servers, and their development activity. However, this information is scattered across directories, package registries, configuration files, and repository histories. We present MCP-Eco, a relational dataset that integrates these sources and links consumer configuration declarations to candidate server projects. Its frozen release contains 16,880,899 records across 19 Parquet tables, covering 78,302 candidate server projects, 16,165 candidate consuming repositories, and 9,200 configuration declarations. Of these declarations, 5,975 resolve to 5,138 distinct repository-server pairs. The dataset also includes tool, resource, and prompt descriptions, declared dependencies, and associated development records, including pull requests, reviews, issues, and commits. Provenance fields distinguish directory-reported capabilities from those observed through live probing and document discovery sources and declaration-matching methods. These connections support research on MCP interface design, configuration practices, and repository maintenance, while enabling practitioners to inspect tool schemas and existing integration configurations. The dataset and accompanying analysis scripts are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/mcp-research-alliance/mcp-ecosystem Demo video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N7TqnNneSfU
case_studies.summary: MCP‑Eco tackles the problem of fragmented information about Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, consumer projects, and their development activity by creating a large relational dataset that links configuration declarations, server projects, and repository history. The team built a 16.9 million‑record Parquet dataset with 19 tables that map consumers to servers, including dependencies and pull‑request data, making it possible to study MCP interface design and integration patterns. The result is a public resource that lets researchers and practitioners explore how MCP tools are configured and maintained, though it does not directly impact everyday cloud infrastructure management.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work
case_studies.score_reasoning: The MCP-Eco dataset is a research artifact that maps LLM agent server ecosystems. While it offers insight into tooling and configuration practices, it does not provide a direct, ready-to-deploy solution for IT engineers managing Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, or cloud infra. The dataset and scripts are released, giving it modest AI maturity, but the opportunity to monetize or apply it within 90 days is limited. Overall, the paper has minimal real-world impact for the target audience.
